planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify seed 4 weeks before spring sowing; since this all-yellow form does not breed true from open-pollinated seed shared with red-flowered wild columbine nearby, isolate plantings or propagate by division to keep the color pure.

directions: This is a naturally occurring color form of eastern wild columbine, found scattered through the species' range, in which the typical red spurs and sepals are replaced entirely by soft butterfly-yellow, so the nodding spring flowers lack any red pigment at all. Specialty native-plant growers occasionally offer seed or plants collected from these yellow-flowered colonies separately from the red-and-yellow wild type, since the trait is recessive and reverts in mixed seed strains. Grow it exactly as the species, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled woodland light, and keep it apart from red-flowered columbine if preserving the clear yellow color matters, since bees readily cross-pollinate the two forms. Like the species it is short-lived but self-sows readily, forming a loose colony of all-yellow plants over a few seasons if isolated.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; one of the older bronze-leaf alumroot selections, predating the modern wave of Heuchera hybrids bred mainly for foliage color.

directions: Bressingham Bronze forms a tidy mound of ruffled, deep bronze-purple leaves that hold their color through summer better than many later hybrids, topped from late spring into summer by wiry stems of small, creamy-white bell flowers that draw bees. Introduced through the long-running Bressingham breeding program in England that also produced well-known Bergenia and Astilbe selections, it predates the wave of Terra Nova-style multi-species Heuchera hybrids and stays closer to the straight species in form and vigor. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, since the leaf color washes out and scorches in hot afternoon sun. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep foliage dense and well colored.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; selected at Montrose Nursery in North Carolina as a richly colored seedling from a 'Palace Purple' population.

directions: Montrose Ruby was selected by Nancy Goodwin at Montrose Nursery in Hillsborough, North Carolina, as an especially dark seedling arising from 'Palace Purple' alumroot, with rounded, deeply veined leaves in a saturated wine-ruby shade overlaid with a faint silvery sheen. Airy, wiry stems carry small, pinkish-white bell flowers above the foliage in late spring, though the plant is grown chiefly for its leaf color rather than its modest bloom. Site it in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, since strong afternoon sun fades the ruby tones and dry shade slows establishment. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to refresh vigor and leaf color.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this selection of the coastal California variety of small-flowered alumroot is grown for its marbled foliage rather than for bloom.

directions: Martha Roderick is a selection of the coastal California variety of small-flowered alumroot, named for the Northern California plantswoman associated with its introduction, and chosen for its rounded, scalloped leaves marbled in silver-gray over olive green rather than for its sparse, pale pink flowers. The low, dense habit and patterned foliage make it a quiet groundcover for shaded rock crevices, stumperies, and the base of ferns and sword ferns, in keeping with the moist, shaded coastal bluffs and redwood-forest margins where the variety grows wild. Give it well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and protection from hot inland sun, which scorches the thinner leaves of this coastal form more readily than inland alumroots. Divide congested clumps in fall or early spring to maintain the tight, patterned rosettes.
